candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.68 probability of malware, and all 20 listed n-grams push toward cryptojacking. The evidence is weak, though. The n-grams are generic x86 mnemonic bigrams for stack and call handling: ADD PUSH (+0.020425), SUB PUSH (+0.017161), CALL PUSH (+0.013568), MOV PUSH (+0.012417), LEA PUSH (+0.011424), PUSH CALL (+0.006988), MOV LEAVE (+0.013228) and LEAVE RET (+0.010632). These are ordinary function prologue, epilogue and argument-passing patterns found in almost all compiled code. No function names, API calls or cryptographic or hashing instruction sequences are given. Nothing here points to mining behavior such as tight arithmetic loops, rotate/shift/XOR-heavy sequences or SIMD usage. Eight of the 20 n-grams have a frequency of 0.000000 (CALL ADD, CMOVZ MOV, ADD POP, CALL CALL, XOR XOR, XOR CALL, CMP CMOVZ, MOV JZ). Their SHAP contributions (+0.006800 to +0.011137) come from their absence in this binary, so they do not show a mining-related construct. XOR XOR and XOR CALL are absent, which argues against a heavy XOR-based hashing routine. MOV MOVSD.REP (+0.012765) and LEA MOVSD.REP (+0.007191) suggest block memory copying or structure initialization at low frequency (0.001845 and 0.003690), which is not specific to cryptojacking. The model leans malware-ward, but the evidence is consistent with generic compiled code and is not conclusive, so the tier is low-confidence.
